questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Friends from Milan spoke very positively about the city’s food culture, vibrant cultural life, and impressive architecture, which strongly attracted me to the destination. In addition, I had heard good things about the academic quality of the university, which confirmed my choice of Milan for my exchange.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I had a good study abroad experience. The food was great and quite affordable, as were drinks, and Milan has a good nightlife. It’s a very beautiful city and easy to get around. Academically, the courses were easier than I expected, which had both upsides and downsides. It gave me more free time, but it was also less challenging than I had hoped. There were many Danish students, so I mostly spent time with them and didn’t make as many Italian friends as expected. Still, it was a positive and enjoyable experience overall.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Finding information upon arrival was about as confusing as it probably is everywhere with Erasmus, as the system can be a bit unclear at first. However, the staff at the international office were very kind and helpful. I didn’t really run into major problems, so I didn’t need much assistance overall.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not receive any specific assistance upon arrival, but the international office staff were available and helpful if needed. Overall, I did not require much support, as I did not experience any major issues.

How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy to find off-campus housing. We found our place through HousingAnywhere, which worked very well overall. The platform has a somewhat high service fee, but it was still worth it, as it allowed us to have our own apartment rather than staying in an Airbnb, which seemed more expensive. We lived slightly outside the city ring, which was completely fine since Milan is easy to get around and public transport works well. My recommendation would be to check that there is a metro line nearby, as living a bit further out is not an issue if transport is convenient.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Start looking for off-campus housing early, as there are some really good apartments available if you are early in the process.

Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process was easy. We simply went to the office, and everything was handled quickly and smoothly.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Staff at the office

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Registering for classes was very easy. In the beginning, I was able to try out several courses and switch between them without any issues, and it did not feel like there was a strict limit on the number of students per class, which reduced a lot of stress. I even changed courses halfway through the exchange, and this worked without any problems. Looking back, we stressed unnecessarily about the process, as it was quite flexible. From a Political Science perspective, there were also more courses that could be approved by my home university than initially expected, which meant we had real choices and were able to take the courses we wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: My main advice would be to check the exam dates and exam formats before choosing courses. We chose courses where the exams finished before Christmas, which worked very well. It is also worth looking at the exam formats, as the oral exams turned out to be much easier than expected. The registration process itself was straightforward and worked smoothly through the university’s website, without any major issues.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They were way easier than expected

questions.answer: BA

questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The overall level of the courses was lower than I had expected. The academic workload was relatively light, and the requirements were generally manageable. This made it easier to balance studies with social life and exploring the city, but it also meant that the courses were less academically demanding than I am used to. Overall, the level was accessible and suitable for exchange students, though perhaps not very challenging.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Compared to UCPH, the teaching style was more similar to classroom-based teaching, with a stronger focus on lectures. In most courses, the lecturer did most of the talking, and student participation was limited and largely optional. This also seemed to vary somewhat between courses. One of the biggest differences was that many courses had mandatory attendance requirements, which we are not used to at UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Multi-Level Legal System
(This year the course changed from 6 to 9 ECTS. On its own, it could be credited as “European Politics”; otherwise, it had to be combined with “European Monetary Law”.)

European Monetary Law
(Credited as “European Politics”.)

Political Order, Violence and Institutions
(Credited as DAK3 at my home university.)

Law and Policies of Social Rights Protection in Europe
(Elective course.)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend the courses I chose, as they turned out to be quite manageable. In particular, I would recommend Political Order, Violence and Institutions, which I found very interesting and well taught. For Political Science students from UCPH, the content aligns well with material we are already familiar with, which makes the course easier to follow. I know some students chose Comparative Political Systems for DAK3, but I personally found it to involve more continuous assignments and workload. Instead, Political Order, Violence and Institutions felt like a better and more balanced option. I would also strongly recommend Law and Policies of Social Rights Protection in Europe, which had an excellent lecturer and was both engaging and well structured.

Multi-Level Legal System and European Monetary Law initially felt quite difficult, mainly because they are law courses, which we were not used to. However, the exams turned out to be quite relaxed, especially European Monetary Law, where the exam was essentially a PowerPoint presentation. I would recommend taking Multi-Level Legal System as a non-attending student, as the lectures were hopeless to follow due to language issues. Unfortunately, there were no real alternatives, as the course was needed to obtain credit for “European Politics” at my home university.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not encounter any major unexpected costs. Food, thrift shopping, and public transport were relatively affordable (I would recommend getting a monthly transport pass). There were no required book purchases. The most expensive costs were entrance fees to clubs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Drinks were cheaper than expected, especially Aperol spritz (for example around 3.5 EUR at Bar Picchio). Otherwise, prices were more or less as expected. Food at supermarkets was slightly cheaper than in Denmark, but not by much.

What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find any major cultural differences particularly challenging. Most differences were easy to adapt to and part of the experience. At times, administrative processes could feel a bit less structured than what I am used to, but nothing that caused real problems. Overall, the cultural differences were manageable and not a major challenge.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Food!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Relax, everything works out. The university in Milan is quite flexible and relaxed, and people are generally willing to help if you need it. There is no need to stress too much about the process.
Be mindful of exams and transport. Oral exams are usually the easiest option, so it’s worth considering this when choosing courses. Getting a monthly metro pass is highly recommended, as public transport makes it easy to get around the city.
Try to engage beyond the Danish bubble. Many courses have WhatsApp groups where both practical information and social activities are shared. Joining these early can help you meet more international and Italian students. It’s also worth exploring thrift shops like Mercatino, which are some of the best and often located slightly outside the city, as well as local markets beyond the well-known ones by the canals.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Some courses may overlap in their schedules, but it is often possible to make it work. I would recommend speaking directly with the lecturers, as they were generally understanding if you missed slightly more classes than formally allowed.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: New friendships<33

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge was the lack of clear information about exams and exam formats, which caused unnecessary stress. In addition, deadlines were sometimes handled quite flexibly by lecturers, which took some getting used to.
